title: Finland got the world’s first licence to bury spent nuclear fuel, 430 metres down
body: On 22 October 2026 the Finnish Government granted the company Posiva the world’s first operating licence for a final repository for spent nuclear fuel: Onkalo, at Olkiluoto in western Finland, about 430 metres down in bedrock some 1,800 million years old. Spent fuel is fiercely radioactive when it leaves a reactor. [According to Posiva](https://www.posiva.fi/en/index/finaldisposal/long-termsafety/spentfuel.html), only a hundredth of that is left after a year and a thousandth after 40 years, but it takes about 250,000 years to fade to the level of a rich uranium ore. So the design stacks barriers that back each other up: the fuel sits in a cast-iron insert inside a welded copper shell 5 cm thick, each canister stands in its own hole about 8 metres deep, packed in **bentonite clay** that swells when wet, and the tunnels are backfilled with clay and sealed with concrete plugs. The licence covers up to 6,500 tonnes of uranium, about 3,300 canisters at no more than 60 a year. Disposal can start only after commissioning tests that Finland’s Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority must approve, and no start date has been given.

slides.question: Spent nuclear fuel has cooled for 40 years after leaving a reactor. What share of its first radioactivity is left?
slides.explanation: About 0.1%, a thousandth. Most of it fades fast: a hundredth is left after one year. The last of it lasts far longer, about 250,000 years to reach the level of a rich uranium ore.

slides.alt: Animation in granite greys and copper: a cross-section down to Onkalo’s tunnels 430 m under Olkiluoto, bars of radioactivity falling to a thousandth, a canister seen from above, cast iron in copper in bentonite clay, lowered into its hole, the tunnel backfilled, then 3,300 squares, one per canister.
slides.music: “Hiding Your Reality” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Let the years pass until the caesium-137 in spent fuel is down to a thousandth. How much plutonium-239 is left by then?
slides.takeaway: About 300 years, ten 30-year half-lives, for caesium-137. Plutonium-239 is still over 99% there: its half-life is 24,110 years, so the barriers must hold far longer.

slides.heading: Barriers at Finland’s Onkalo store, inside out

steps.label: Copper shell, 5 cm thick, welded shut
Bentonite clay swells to seal the hole

slides.heading: Each barrier covers for the others
slides.text: In the design of Posiva, the company that built Onkalo, the copper keeps groundwater off the iron and the cast iron takes the weight. The bentonite cushions each canister against small rock movements and, if one ever broke, would slow any escape. Its safety case even looks at ice ages over the next million years.

slides.question: Why is each canister at Onkalo packed in bentonite clay?
options: It swells when wet and seals gaps
It absorbs all of the radiation
It lets the canister be dug up
slides.explanation: Bentonite swells when it gets wet, filling the space between the rock and the canister. It cushions small rock movements and would slow down any leak.
